name: yume-en-ipa
about: How her phone voice reads English: one table, read by en_phonemize.py (training) and by the phone's EnglishPhonemes.kt (to come), so both give the voice the same phoneme codepoints.

English goes to IPA in the style espeak-ng en-us writes (the style her base voice, Piper hifi_tts_92, learned): stress mark right before the stressed vowel, length marks, diphthongs as two codepoints, no flapping, no glottal stops.
Every emitted symbol is one codepoint of the voice's tokens.txt. g is U+0261 (ASCII g is another id).
Japanese stays Japanese: kana and kanji, her romaji words (ja_words) and Latin words that read only as romaji go through Open JTalk exactly as before.
The rules for splitting a line into sentences and segments, and for joining them, are in 'segmentation' and 'boundaries'; mix_phonemize.py is the reference implementation.

cmudict.rule: Lines 'word PH PH ...'; text after '#' is a comment; a word with '(' is a variant and is skipped; the first entry of a word wins. Lookup is by the lowercased word.

r_vowel_before_vowel.about: ER right before another vowel inside a word (hurry, every, worry) keeps its r for that vowel, as espeak writes it.

stress_rule: The mark goes right before the stressed vowel's IPA (espeak style): 'hello' həlˈoʊ. Stress 0 has no mark. IY0 is short i (espeak's happY vowel); IY1 and IY2 are iː.

weak_forms.about: Function words, said reduced and unstressed. 'strong' is used when the word ends its sentence (where you from?, yes i am): the last word of an English segment that is the sentence's last segment. Words without 'strong' are always weak.

word_overrides.about: ARPAbet, before the CMU dictionary. '_' is a word break. Her typed contractions without apostrophes, chat words (typed lowercase: dm, bf, rn, said the way people say them aloud), units after a number (cm, km, kg), and words CMU lacks or reads wrong for her.

caps_as_letters.about: Words typed in capitals (2-5 letters) that are said letter by letter even though CMU or an override has them as a word (CM is a TV ad in Japan; cm after a number is centimeters).

letters.w: D AH1 B AH0 L Y UW0

letters_rule: Letter names of one word join into one word; every letter but the last has its stress 1 turned into 2 (DJ: dˌiːdʒˈeɪ).

ja_words.about: Latin words that are her Japanese (romaji), her people's names, Japanese places and family names, and Japanese words CMU would take for English (dake, kono, sensei, Ginza, Tanaka). Genuinely English spellings (are, no, so, sake, kimono) stay English. Always read the Japanese way: the kana (kanji for a place name Open JTalk reads better that way) go to Open JTalk.

numbers.about: Digits read in English when the nearest word after them, or else before them, in the same sentence is English; otherwise they stay in the Japanese text for Open JTalk. A Japanese run with no letter or digit (°, ※, ＾) is not a word here.
numbers.ordinal_rule: Spell the cardinal, then change its last word: ordinal_words, else a final y becomes ieth, else add th.
numbers.time_rule: h:mm: hour, then minutes; :00 is o'clock; :01-:09 is oh and the digit.
numbers.leading_zero_rule: A number of two or more digits that starts with 0 is read digit by digit (zero for 0).
numbers.always_english: A number with an ordinal suffix (1st) or a $ or € sign is always read in English.
numbers.time_words_rule: am or pm right after a number read in English (7am, 7 pm) is said as letters.

symbols.about: Symbols said as a word in an English segment.

suffixes.about: For a word that is neither an override nor in CMU: strip a suffix, find the base in the overrides or CMU, add the suffix's phones. Tried in this order; the first base found wins. 'drop' letters come off the end, 'append' goes on, 'double' needs the base's last letter to be doubled in the word (stopping -> stop).

compound.about: A word still unknown is split in two, longest first part first, each part at least min_part letters and an override or in CMU. The parts are read as one word.

held_letter.about: A letter held 4 or more times is cut to 3 (KanaText's rule). A word not found then is looked up with each run of 3 cut to 1, then to 2 (NOOO -> no; the persona normalizer has already cut her lowercase words).

latin_word_route.about: Order in which a Latin word is read. The first step that knows it wins.
order: caps: a word typed in capitals, 2-5 letters, in caps_as_letters, or (with the held-letter cuts) in none of weak_forms, overrides and CMU -> English letter names
weak_forms -> English (weak, or strong when it ends the sentence)
CMU (as typed lowercase; then the held-letter cuts) -> English
romaji (the whole word reads as strict romaji, KanaText's Romaji.toHiragana) -> Japanese (hiragana)
else -> Japanese (KanaText's Romaji.toKatakanaLoose, as a Japanese speaker reads an unknown name)
latin_word_route.apostrophes: Curly apostrophes inside a word become '. A word is letters with ' or - between letters. Hyphenated words are read as separate words. A leading or trailing ' is dropped.
latin_word_route.word_chars: ASCII letters after plain_latin: full-width letters made ASCII, combining marks after a Latin letter removed (NFD, strip, NFC).

about: 2. Split into sentences: Piper's _split_sentences pattern, plus an ASCII '.' that is followed by optional closers and then whitespace or the end, is not part of '..' and does not end an abbreviation or dotted letters (dotted_letters). Each sentence keeps its trailing punctuation.

3. Tokenize a sentence: joined word (joined_words), dotted letters (dotted_letters), Latin word, number (digits with , . : inside, ordinal suffix, ¥ $ € before, % after), space, English punctuation, Japanese run (any other character).
4. Peel ja_edge_punct off both ends of each Japanese run into punctuation tokens.
5. Route each Latin word (latin_word_route) and each number (numbers.about).
6. Segments: maximal runs of tokens of one route; English punctuation and Japanese edge punctuation between two segments is the boundary between them.

7. A Japanese segment's text is the sentence's own characters from its first to its last token, with Japanese-route Latin words replaced by their kana and the whitespace next to those words removed; the last segment also gets the sentence's trailing punctuation. It goes to Open JTalk (Piper's JapanesePhonemizer) and its sentences are concatenated.

8. Join: see boundaries. A Japanese segment Open JTalk gives nothing for (※, ＾, °) is left out: no boundary of its own, the segments around it join as if it were not there, and the sentence's last segment that gives phonemes decides the strong form and the end mark.
segmentation.dotted_letters: Single letters each followed by '.' ([A-Za-z](\.[A-Za-z])+ and an optional last '.', not followed by a letter: a.m., e.g., U.S.A.) are one Latin word with the dots dropped, always English: am/pm right after an English number are time_words, else an override of the letters if there is one, else the letter names (letters_rule). Its last '.' never ends a sentence.

joined_words.about: Latin words typed with a mark inside that are one word (matched lowercased at a word start, not followed by a letter), read as the word given.

rules: English words in one segment are joined by one space. A clause mark between them is ',' then a space (espeak style: none before it).
A Japanese segment that is not the last of its sentence loses its final '.' or '?' (Open JTalk ends every piece with one).
Between two segments: ',' and a space when a clause mark stands between them, else one space.
Sentence end: after an English last segment, the sentence's terminal mark ('?' or '!' if it has one, else '.'); after a Japanese last segment nothing is added (Open JTalk's own '.' or '?').
A clause mark at the start of a sentence, or right before its end, is dropped.
Each sentence becomes one phoneme list (one id sequence with its own ^ and $ in Piper).
